title: Asteroid Bennu is so loose that a NASA probe would have sunk into it

cover.alt: Black-and-white view from OSIRIS-REx’s camera: the round sampler head on the end of its arm, just above a surface of jumbled dark rocks and boulders.

body: Bennu, about **490 m** across, seems to be not one solid rock but a rubble pile: boulders and gravel loosely gathered together. Its bulk density is only slightly more than water’s, which suggests that a large share of its inside is empty gaps. When OSIRIS-REx touched it on 20 October 2020 to grab a sample, analysis showed the particles are loosely packed and lightly bound, and that the spacecraft would have sunk in had it not fired its thrusters to back away at once.

slides.alt: Black-and-white camera view of the sampler head on OSIRIS-REx’s arm closing in on a rocky surface; on contact, a bright cloud of rocks and dust bursts out and fills the frame.
slides.caption: 20 October 2020: the sampler head on the arm of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx probe touches Bennu, and rocks and dust fly everywhere as the spacecraft backs away.
slides.credit: NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona · Public domain · excerpt

slides.text: Its predicted macroporosity is about 40%, give or take 10: that much of its volume may be gaps between the rubble.

The sample capsule lands on Earth

slides.question: Roughly how much of Bennu did OSIRIS-REx bring back to Earth?
slides.explanation: About 120 grams of mostly very dark material, landed in a capsule in September 2023 and now being studied around the world.
